title: Firouzja Snaps Nakamura's Streak, Outscores Six Super-GMs
summary: GM Hikaru Nakamura's record-breaking victory streak in the Bullet Brawl arena has finally come to an end after GM Alireza Firouzja stormed home to snatch first place in the 232-strong player event on Saturday. Firouzja finished on 170 points, four ahead of Nakamura and a further seven ahead of GM Ediz Gurel. GM Matthias Bluebaum rounded out the top four, while WIM Melika Mohammadi captured the $100 best women's prize. The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, November 7, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings

title: Bavarian Championship: Few surprises in the opening rounds at Tegernsee
summary:
Fifty players remain on perfect scores after two rounds of the Bavarian Chess Championship, which has attracted 548 participants to Gmund am Tegernsee. Most of the leading seeds have made a strong start, though Jaime Santos, Leonardo Costa and Peter Acs - all among the top ten in the starting rank - were held to draws by lower-rated opponents. Top seed Frederik Svane (pictured) and third seed Alexander Donchenko are among those sharing the lead with 2/2 points. | Photo: Official website

Fifty co-leaders on 2/2 in the 548-player field

The 29 th Open International Bavarian Chess Championship is underway in Gmund am Tegernsee, with 548 participants competing in a nine-round Swiss tournament from 31 October to 8 November. The event, held at Gut Kaltenbrunn on the northern shore of Lake Tegernsee, uses accelerated pairings according to the Baku method during the first five rounds. After two days of play, 50 participants remain on perfect scores, including top seed Frederik Svane and third seed Alexander Donchenko.

The opening round saw most of the leading contenders collect full points. Svane, rated 2662, defeated Julian Wagner with the black pieces, while Donchenko (2610) beat another player named Wagner, Hans. Second seed Jaime Santos Latasa (2626) also started with a win, overcoming Martin Wecker.

There were, however, a few surprises. Reigning German champion Leonardo Costa was held to a draw by 15-year-old Nicola Salsa, despite having a rating advantage of more than 400 points. Young German IM Hussain Besou also dropped half a point, drawing with Martin Böhm, while Hungarian GM Adam Kozak could only draw against Kai Renner.

Julian Wagner 0-1 Frederik Svane

Annotations by Martina Gerdts

Julian Wagner v. Frederik Svane | Photo: Official website

Hans Wagner v. Alexander Donchenko | Photo: Official website

In Sunday's second round, two players from the top ten seeds conceded draws against considerably lower-rated opponents. Santos, the winner of the tournament's 2021 edition, was held by 20-year-old German FM Cedric Chassard (2276), who entered the event as the 68 th seed. On board six, seventh seed Peter Acs (2554) drew with German IM Christian Maier (2229), the 85 th seed. The 67-year-old Maier has considerable experience, having played in the Bundesliga as far back as the early 1980s.

Meanwhile, Svane defeated German WGM Kateryna Dolzhykova, who adopted an aggressive approach but eventually saw her attack repelled. Donchenko survived a complicated time scramble to secure his second victory, while Nijat Abasov, Elham Amar, Valery Kazakouski and Kacper Piorun also maintained perfect scores.

The day included a minor logistical mishap for several of the favourites: Svane, Donchenko and Abasov were among a group of players who missed their bus stop on the way to the venue. They arrived seven minutes late, but all three went on to win their games.

Among the 50 co-leaders are two women, IM Klaudia Kulon and Zuzanna Sobczak.

The third round, scheduled for Monday at 16:00 local time , will see Svane face Chinese IM Jin Yueheng (2355) with the black pieces on board one. Donchenko will also have black against FM Melis Mamatov (2345) on board two, while third board features Azerbaijani GM Nijat Abasov (2580) against German FM Martin Forchert (2332).

title: Vasily Panov: An influential theoretician with a dark side
summary:
Born on 1 November 1906, Vasily Panov was not among the leading Soviet chess players of his generation. However, he was a prominent figure as an author and theoretician. Many players know his name as the inventor of the Panov Attack, which was named after him. Yet Panov's career also had a darker side.

Vasily Nikolayevich Panov was born on 1 November 1906 in Kozelsk, a town in the Kaluga region, south-west of Moscow. His father, Nikolai Alexandrovich Panov, was a finance official, while his mother, Yevgenia Vasilyevna Panova (née Assonova), was the daughter of a well-known local historian and worked as a teacher. Vasily Panov grew up in Kaluga. In 1916, the family moved to Moscow.

Vasily Panov as a player

Vasily Panov learned to play chess from his father at the age of seven. At fifteen, he played in his first tournaments in Moscow.

As a young man, he scored a victory in a simultaneous exhibition given by world champion José Raúl Capablanca.

In 1929, Panov became Moscow champion, while in 1935 and 1939 he finished runner-up. He won bronze in 1941 and 1946.

Panov's greatest tournament success was his victory in the semifinal of the USSR Championship in Kyiv in 1938. In total, Panov qualified for the final of the USSR Championship five times between 1935 and 1948. His best finish was eleventh place in 1939.

In 1950, FIDE awarded Panov the title of international master (IM).

After 1957, Panov took part in tournaments only rarely because of poor health. He played his last tournament in 1963. After that he retired from tournament chess, although he made one final tournament appearance in Skopje in 1970.

During the 1920s, Panov at times followed the example of his older brother N.N. Panov, a poet and author of seafaring stories, and published several poems and feuilleton pieces, often related to chess, in the newspaper Rabochaya Moskva under the pseudonym "Pila". He even wrote a play during this period.

During the Second World War, Panov gave simultaneous exhibitions and lectures for patients in Moscow hospitals.

Vasily Panov as an author and theoretician

As a chess author, Panov published instructional books as well as biographies of well-known masters such as Chigorin, Capablanca and Alekhine. From 1942 to 1965, he was the chess correspondent for the newspaper Izvestia . He also published articles in the youth magazine Pionerskaya Pravda .

In his articles and lessons, Panov was an uncompromising and at times caustic dogmatist. Contemporaries described him as quarrelsome, but also quite humorous. He produced his articles and theoretical studies with great diligence and thoroughness. He had considerable difficulty dealing with defeats in his own games, however.

In his time, every form of journalism, even chess reporting, was closely shaped by the ideological and political aims of the state leadership. Thus, the articles of Panov, who was a party member, including even his book reviews, were permeated by the communist ideology of the period.

As only became known later, however, Panov went even further in his political dogmatism. He was an informer. Gennadi Sosonko reported for New in Chess (2014/3), in his article "The Panov Attack", that in 1950, while reviewing a book on the Open Games by Paul Keres, Panov accused the author of spreading "bourgeois-Western" and "anti-Marxist" theories. A corresponding letter was found in the KGB archives after the collapse of the USSR. Besides political dogmatism, resentment and envy were probably also motives behind Vasily Panov's actions in this case.

Keres had played tournaments in the German Reich during the Nazi era and, when Estonia was occupied by the Red Army in 1945, attempted to flee to Finland. He was arrested, however, and narrowly escaped deportation to Siberia. Keres had to come to terms with the new rulers.

In his newspaper articles, Panov also frequently presented himself as a kind of "chess inquisitor", denouncing "anti-Marxist tendencies" and "rootless cosmopolitanism" and calling for a political cleansing of chess literature.

The attack had no immediate consequences for Keres. As a world-class player, he was too valuable to Soviet propaganda. The Estonian answered over the board: he won the USSR Championship in 1950.

Vasily Panov achieved major success with his publications and theoretical investigations into the openings. Here, Panov developed many new ideas. The best-known opening named after him is the variation of the Caro-Kann Defence arising after 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.cxd5 cxd5 4.c4 , the so-called Panov Attack.

Against the Scheveningen Variation of the Sicilian Defence, Panov investigated a set-up for White with 6.g3 followed by a bishop fianchetto. The attacking idea with 6.g4 against the Scheveningen also originated with Panov before it was adopted by Paul Keres in the 1940s and named after the Estonian. Perhaps Panov's dislike of Keres even stemmed from this.

Panov also investigated plans for White in the Modern Variation against the Alekhine Defence (4.Nf3 followed by h3) and a set-up with ...Bb7 in the Chigorin Variation of the Ruy Lopez.

After 1.d4 , Panov advocated the defence for Black with 1…c5 2.d5 e5 3.e4 d6 4.c4 Nf6 5.Nc3 Be7 (or, by transposition, 1…Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4 Be7), which later became known as the Czech Benoni.

Panov, a cat lover

Vasily Panov died on 18 January 1973 in Moscow. He was buried at Moscow's Vostryakovskoye Cemetery (Central Cemetery), section 32, in the family grave.
